newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican "formal" employment grows 7.9 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Mexican "formal" employment grows 7.9 pct in 1996.

text.p: "Formal" employment grew in Mexico by 7.9 percent in 1996 compared with levels in 1995, the director of the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) said Wednesday.

"The number of permanent insured workers (via IMSS) is 9,163,459, a record figure for the institute and which has been achieved thanks to the exceptional recovery of the labor force (demand) in this country," Genaro Borrego said. "Last year formal employment grew 7.9 percent."
Borrego, giving an annual report before President Ernesto Zedillo, said 661,024 formal jobs were created in 1996, which he said was 274,493 more than those lost in the crisis year of 1995.
Mexico records "formal" employment because a large portion of the labor force is "informally" employed in jobs such as street vendors, shoe shiners and home help.
Estimates vary widely about what percentage of the active Mexican workforce falls into the informal sector, but most suggest it is at least 30 percent.
Mexico's crisis, sparked by an abrupt devaluation in December 1994, badly affected employment as the economy took a nosedive and companies trimmed workforces.
